title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Angioplasty stands as a minimally invasive solution for significant blockages in blood vessels, aiming to restore blood flow to deprived tissues. Its application extends to various vessels throughout the body. The procedure calls for an array of tools like access site sheaths, guiding catheters, guide wires, balloons, and stents, tailored to specific angioplasty types. Typically conducted in cardiac and peripheral catheterization labs, as well as hybrid operating rooms, this intervention, while minimally invasive, isn't immune to complications. This overview delves into indications, contraindications, equipment, techniques, and the crucial roles of personnel and interprofessional collaboration in enhancing procedural success.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Introduction
content: Atherosclerosis is the most common pathology behind stenotic blood vessels. Atherosclerotic vascular disease is the most common cause of morbidity and mortality in the USA and worldwide. It commonly manifests as coronary artery disease, carotid artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, and renal artery stenosis. [1] [2] Angioplasty ("angio" meaning "vessel, and "plastics" meaning "molding")  is a minimally invasive endovascular procedure for hemodynamically significant stenosis to restore blood flow to ischemic tissues. Recent advances in the interventional armamentarium, techniques, and training have made it possible to treat almost all anatomic lesions with endovascular means. Dr.Charles Dotter performed the first angioplasty in 1964. Interventional armamentariums and angioplasty techniques have greatly evolved in the last 60 years. [3] [4] [5] Even though angioplasty can be performed in many stenosed blood vessels, we mainly focus on coronary, carotid, and peripheral artery disease.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Atherosclerosis is characterized by forming fibrofatty plaques consisting of cholesterol-laden macrophages, calcium, fibrous tissue, tissue matrix, and cellular debris deposits in the intima of blood vessels. [6] When this plaque increases in size, it disrupts blood flow resulting in characteristic symptoms of distal ischemia. An acute rise in this plaque size, e.g., due to hemorrhage into the plaque or rupture followed by platelet-rich thrombus formation, results in acute ischemia and risks distal necrosis.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Angioplasty aims to compress the plaque with a balloon or stent and open the stenosed artery to relieve distal ischemia. Once the access sheath is placed within the preferred artery, typically the radial or common femoral artery, proceduralists advance diagnostic or guide catheters of various sizes, shapes, and diameters to the target artery. Intravenous contrast medium is then injected to delineate the coronary, peripheral, and carotid arteries. Upon defining the anatomy and identifying hemodynamically significant stenosis, interventionalists proceed with intervention. They select wires based on their size, thickness, shape, tip strength, and characteristics, along with appropriate medications. Balloons are introduced to dilate the narrowed blood vessel, and we deploy drug-coated balloons, drug-eluting stents, or bioabsorbable stents as per indications and vessel characteristics. Once the intervention is complete and blood flow is restored, we remove all wires, balloons, and catheters, ensuring secure hemostasis.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Indications -- Coronary Angioplasty and Stent Placement
content: Acute coronary syndromes: Unstable angina, STEMI, and NSTEMI. In stable coronary artery disease, indications for PCI are: Activity limiting symptoms despite optimal medical therapy, Active patients who prefer PCI for improvement in the quality of life, and single-vessel disease involving right coronary and left circumflex coronary arteries or two-vessel disease involving right coronary and left circumflex arteries. For left main disease or multivessel disease in patients who have diabetes - CABG is preferred over PCI. [7] [8] [9]

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Indications -- Carotid Angioplasty
content: Revascularization is primarily indicated in patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis of >70% to 99%. [10] [11] In general carotid endarterectomy has less peri-procedure stroke rates than stenting. [12] Patient subgroups with better outcomes with carotid stenting are - Prior neck irradiation, high cervical carotid bifurcation, or 100% occlusion of the contralateral internal carotid artery.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Indications -- Peripheral Vascular Disease
content: Despite lifestyle adjustment, supervised exercise programs, and pharmacotherapy, patients with disabling symptoms are candidates for revascularization. The choice of revascularization procedure depends on symptomatology, patient risk, location and extent of disease, comorbidities, functional status, and preference. Angioplasty with stenting is the preferred procedure except in cases of - Eccentric calcified stenosis, a long segment of stenosis, or multifocal stenosis. [13] [14]

content: Angioplasty with stenting is the preferred treatment for patients with renovascular disease with uncontrolled hypertension despite maximally tolerated medical therapy.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Contraindications
content: General contraindications of angioplasty procedure are small size vessels, posterior calcification, occlusion, or hematoma of dishes, inability to tolerate dual antiplatelet therapy or allergy to stent components. Carotid angioplasty is relatively contraindicated in the elderly (>80y.o) due to the high risk of stroke. [16] A relative contraindication includes significant comorbidities that severely limit life expectancy.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Equipment
content: We need the following equipment: Fluoroscopy and X-ray imaging equipment (including a radiographic table, two X-ray tubes, fluoroscopy screen) Micropuncture needle (18-20G) Hydrophilic sheath Contrast material Guidewire Balloon catheter The stent of an appropriate type and size Ultrasound imaging device Hemodynamic monitoring system Some of the types of stents used are: 1. Coronary angioplasty Bare metal stent Drug-eluting stent Early generation drug-eluting stents: Sirolimus-eluting stent and Paclitaxel-eluting stent Durable polymer drug-eluting stents: Everolimus-eluting stent, Zotarolimus eluting stent, Ridaforolimus-eluting stent Bioabsorbable polymer drug-eluting stents Thin-strut bioabsorbable polymer DES Ultra-thin strut DES: Orsiro stent Polymer free DES Others: Combo stent - sirolimus elution from the biodegradable polymer matrix, which is abluminal in shape with a CD34 antibody layer

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Equipment
content: The choice of stent depends on local availability and the interventional cardiologist's expertise - Everolimus-eluting stents, Zotarolimus-eluting stents, ridaforolimus-eluting stents, and biodegradable stents are usually the first choice. A bare-metal stent is preferred in cases where the patient is actively bleeding, or the duration of dual antiplatelet therapy cannot be >30 days, e.g., non-cardiac surgery within 4-6 weeks of PCI. However, recent updates suggest that certain drug-eluting stents now necessitate only 1-3 months of dual antiplatelet therapy. Consequently, the utilization of bare metal stents has become very rare in contemporary practice. 2. title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Preparation
content: The vascular surgeon/ interventional cardiologist evaluates the patient to determine eligibility and the most appropriate procedure (plain angioplasty, stent placement, type of stent, atherectomy). Usually, this does not require anesthesia and, therefore, does not require pre-procedure evaluation by an anesthesiologist unless the patient has a high Mallampati score. When involved, an anesthesiologist evaluates the patient's determination of the risk of the procedure and assessment to optimize medication and medical conditions.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Preparation
content: Evaluating patient allergies (to iodinated contrast) and medication compliance is critical. It is essential to assess renal function in these patients as these procedures require a significant amount of contrast material for appropriate visualization throughout the process. Preoperatively, any nephrotoxic medications are held, including NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, loop diuretics, and metformin.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Preparation
content: Anticoagulants (warfarin, rivaroxaban, apixaban) are also withheld before surgery, and the patient is premedicated with aspirin alone or in combination with ticagrelor/ prasugrel/clopidogrel. The patient is made NPO for 8-12hr before the procedure. A few hours before the process, the patient is evaluated for hemodynamic stability and monitored continuously throughout the course. The procedure area is prepared by shaving the target area, antiseptic application, and drapes are placed around the target access site. Angioplasty is performed under moderate to deep sedation for most adult patients, but pediatric patients may require general anesthesia.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Technique or Treatment
content: Radial artery: After palpation of the radial artery 2cm proximal to the radial styloid process, an arteriotomy incision is made. Next, a micropuncture needle is used to puncture the radial artery, and a hydrophilic sheath is introduced into the artery by the modified Selinger technique. Subsequently, a vasodilator is injected into the artery (usually nicardipine 500 µg or verapamil 5 mg along with nitroglycerine IV heparin 50 U/kg or Max 5000U is given to reduce the risk of radial artery thrombosis.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Technique or Treatment
content: Femoral artery: After palpation of the common femoral artery, 2cm below the center of the inguinal ligament at the point of maximum palpable impulse, an arteriotomy incision is made. Fluoroscopy can be used for better localization of the femoral artery in the middle of the femoral head. Subsequently, a micropuncture needle is used to enter the femoral artery, and a hydrophilic sheath is placed with a modified Selinger technique.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Technique or Treatment
content: After obtaining access, a guidewire is inserted into the artery into the target vessel. A balloon-tipped catheter is then advanced over the guidewire to the target site. When the target artery is reached, contrast (usually iohexol) is injected into the system, followed by imaging to visualize the arterial system and obtain a pre-procedure angiogram. The catheter is then advanced through the artery's stenotic segment and inflated to dilate the target artery and compress the atherosclerotic plaque. If an atherectomy is planned, then the atherectomy device is introduced through the guidewire, and the plaque is disrupted (mechanical) or ablated (laser) at this point.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Technique or Treatment
content: If stenting is planned, the catheter is withdrawn after balloon dilation, and a stent of appropriate size and diameter is advanced over the guidewire. Once the stent is in the desired artery, contrast material is injected, and the stent is positioned and deployed across the lesion, followed by another angiography. Intravascular imaging tools like Intravascular ultrasonography or Optic coherence tomography are used to assess the adequacy of stent deployment, including stent expansion and apposition. If post-stent deployment angiograms are deemed adequate, the guidewire is withdrawn. Hemostasis is achieved by direct manual compression or applying a compression band to the wrist (radial) or vascular closure devices (femoral).

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Complications
content: Complications of coronary angiography and intervention can include: Bleeding or hematoma at the catheter insertion site. Allergic reactions to contrast dye, though rare. Blood vessel damage or dissection. Arrhythmias (abnormal heart rhythms). Heart attack or stroke, particularly in individuals with pre-existing heart disease. Infection at the catheter insertion site. Kidney damage, especially in those with pre-existing kidney problems. Rarely, contrast-induced nephropathy (a type of kidney damage due to the contrast dye). Rarely, embolization of plaque or blood clots leads to blockages in other blood vessels. Very rarely, severe complications such as coronary artery perforation or cardiac tamponade (compression of the heart due to fluid buildup around it). title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Complications
content: Bleeding or hematoma at the site where the catheter was inserted. Allergic reactions to the contrast dye, although these are rare. Blood vessel damage or dissection. Formation of blood clots at the catheter insertion site or within the blood vessels. Infection at the catheter insertion site. Kidney damage or contrast-induced nephropathy, particularly in individuals with pre-existing kidney problems. Embolization of plaque or blood clots leads to blockages in other blood vessels. Rarely, arterial perforation or pseudoaneurysm formation. Neurological complications, such as stroke, if the procedure involves the arteries supplying blood to the brain. Very rarely, severe complications such as compartment syndrome (increased pressure within muscles), arterial thrombosis (blood clot within an artery), or allergic reactions to medications used during the procedure.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Clinical Significance
content: Angioplasty procedures are a minimally invasive alternative to an open surgical approach for arterial stenosis. As a result, these procedures carry significantly lower morbidity and mortality with a shorter duration of hospital stay and recovery with an acceptable risk of restenosis. Percutaneous coronary angioplasty has revolutionized the treatment of MI and unstable angina and is now the standard of care. Stenting and angioplasty are acceptable alternatives for peripheral vascular disease for suitable indications and have better recovery rates at the cost of lower revascularization rates. Carotid angioplasty procedures, however, have more risk than benefit in comparison to carotid endarterectomy procedures and are advisable only in a select group of patients. The overall success of the interventions is also enhanced by patient compliance with diet, exercise, medications, smoking cessation, and medical optimization of comorbidities.

title: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty and Balloon Catheters -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Angioplasty is a complex procedure requiring a high level of training of the performing surgeon/radiologist/cardiologist. Improved outcomes are observed in physicians trained with a higher procedural volume.
